conversation.assistant:
you’re not dumb, this stuff is just taught in the most confusing way possible 😭

think of big O as: “how fast does this thing get slower as the input gets bigger?”

imagine you have a stack of books:

- O(1): you grab the top book. done. doesn’t matter if there are 10 or 10 million books.
- O(n): you check every book one by one. more books = more time.
- O(n²): you check every book, and for each one you check all the others again. this blows up fast.

now the weird one:

O(n log n)

this is like… you don’t look at every book one-by-one in a dumb way. you keep splitting the pile in half.

example: finding a name in a sorted phone book  
- instead of flipping page by page (O(n)), you open in the middle  
- then cut the remaining half again  
- and again, and again  

that “keep cutting in half” part is the “log n”

so O(n log n) usually means:
- you do something for all n items  
- but each step is sped up by this “cutting in half” trick  

a classic example is merge sort:
- split stuff in half (log n levels)
- process all n items at each level  
→ total = n * log n

now amortized (this one trips everyone up):

amortized just means: “on average over time, not worst-case for one operation”

example: dynamic array (like Python list)

- most of the time, adding an item is O(1)
- BUT sometimes it runs out of space and has to copy everything → O(n)

that sounds bad, right? but it doesn’t happen often.

so if you average it out over many adds, each one is still basically O(1). that’s amortized O(1).

so:
- worst-case: one operation might be expensive  
- amortized: spread that cost over many cheap ones  

quick mental cheats for exams:
- see a single loop → O(n)
- nested loops → probably O(n²)
- “cut in half each time” → O(log n)
- sorting with divide-and-conquer → usually O(n log n)
- occasional expensive resize → amortized

if you want, i can throw you a few practice problems and walk through them step-by-step so it actually sticks before your midterm 👍
